people.name: Gaius Memmius (tribune 111)
people.summary: Tribune of 111 who denounced the Senate's dealings with Jugurtha and had him summoned to Rome under safe conduct; Sallust gives him a fierce speech against the nobility. Clubbed to death in 100 while standing for the consulship against Glaucia.
people.death: killed by supporters of Saturninus and Glaucia at the consular elections

people.name: Quintus Varius Hybrida
people.summary: Tribune of 90 from Sucro in Spain (hence 'Hybrida', the half-breed), whose lex Varia set up a court to try those who had encouraged the Italian revolt, striking at Drusus' friends. Condemned under his own law in 89 and, Cicero says, died in agony.

people.name: Ariobarzanes I of Cappadocia
people.summary: Cappadocian noble chosen king about 95 under Roman supervision and installed by Sulla; expelled by Mithridates or Tigranes at least three times and restored by Rome each time. His epithet Philoromaios ('friend of the Romans') summed up the role of the Anatolian client kings. Abdicated in favour of his son about 63.

people.name: Publius Vettius Scato
people.summary: Marsic or Paelignian commander in the Social War who defeated Perperna and the consul Lucius Caesar in 90. Captured in 89, he was killed by his own slave, who stabbed him to save him from humiliation and then killed himself. Cicero recalls his courteous meeting with Pompeius Strabo between the lines.

people.name: Lucius Julius Caesar (consul 90)
people.summary: Consul of 90 who commanded on the southern front of the Social War and carried the lex Julia granting citizenship to loyal Latin and Italian communities, the decisive political concession of the war. Censor in 89; murdered in the Marian massacres of 87 with his brother Gaius Julius Caesar Strabo.
people.death: killed in the Marian massacres, his head displayed on the Rostra

people.name: Marius Egnatius
people.summary: Samnite commander in the Social War who took Venafrum by treachery in 90 and defeated Lucius Caesar near Teanum. Killed in battle in 89. Velleius lists him among the leading commanders of the Italian confederation.

people.name: Gaius Vidacilius
people.summary: Picene commander from Asculum who defeated Pompeius Strabo near Firmum in 90 and fought his way into besieged Asculum. When the town's fall was imminent he executed his political opponents, built his own pyre in a temple, took poison at a banquet and had himself burned.

people.name: Lucius Porcius Cato (consul 89)
people.summary: Great-grandson of Cato the Censor. As praetor in 90 he subdued Etruria, and as consul in 89 fought the Marsi with some success before being killed attacking their camp by the Fucine Lake, according to one tradition by the younger Marius.
people.death: killed in battle against the Marsi near the Fucine Lake

people.name: Quintus Pompeius Rufus
people.summary: Sulla's colleague as consul in 88, whose son married Sulla's daughter and was killed in the Sulpician riots. He joined Sulla's march on Rome, then was sent to take over Pompeius Strabo's army in Picenum and murdered by the soldiers.
people.death: murdered by Pompeius Strabo's soldiers while sacrificing

people.name: Nicomedes IV Philopator
people.summary: King of Bithynia from about 94, twice expelled by Mithridates and restored by Rome. His raid on Pontus at Roman instigation in 89 started the First Mithridatic War. The young Caesar's stay at his court in 80 gave rise to lasting gibes about Caesar as 'the queen of Bithynia'. He bequeathed his kingdom to Rome.

people.name: Aristion
people.summary: Philosopher, said to have been a Peripatetic or Epicurean, who led Athens into alliance with Mithridates in 88 and ruled as tyrant during Sulla's siege, mocking the Romans from the walls. Captured on the Acropolis after the sack and executed.
people.death: executed on Sulla's orders after the fall of the Acropolis

people.name: Lucius Cornelius Merula
people.summary: Flamen Dialis, made suffect consul in 87 when Cinna was deposed. When Marius and Cinna took the city he opened his veins on the Capitol, leaving a note that he had removed his priestly cap first so as not to pollute it.

people.name: Gaius Norbanus
people.summary: Tribune of 103 who prosecuted Caepio for Arausio, defended in 95 by Marcus Antonius. As consul in 83 he was beaten by Sulla at Mount Tifata and again at Faventia in 82. Fled to Rhodes and killed himself when Sulla demanded his surrender.

people.name: Quintus Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus
people.summary: Son of the victor of Vercellae, consul in 78 with Lepidus, whose revolt he defeated outside Rome in 77. He rebuilt and dedicated the Capitoline temple (69) and the Tabularium, opposed the lex Gabinia and Manilia, and as princeps senatus led the optimates until his death; he lost the election for pontifex maximus to Caesar in 63.
people.detail: Catulus was the model of the upright Sullan noble: he refused bribes, defended the Senate's authority and was widely respected even by opponents. When he asked the people in 67 whom they would turn to if Pompey died, they shouted 'You!'. His humiliation by the young Caesar in the pontifical election, despite offering Caesar a bribe to withdraw, marked the arrival of a new generation.

people.name: Gaius Herennius
people.summary: Sertorius' legate in eastern Spain, tribune in 80 who had blocked a bill restoring Pompey's father's allies. Defeated and killed by Pompey before Valentia in 75.

people.name: Lucius Afranius
people.summary: Picene follower of Pompey who served him in Spain against Sertorius, in the East, and as consul in 60, elected by open bribery. Commanded Pompey's Spanish legions with Petreius in 49, surrendered at Ilerda, rejoined Pompey, and after Thapsus was captured and killed by Sittius' troops.

people.name: Gaius Cornelius (tribune 67)
people.summary: Former quaestor of Pompey; as tribune in 67 proposed laws against lending to foreign envoys and against Senate dispensations, and carried the lex Cornelia binding praetors to their edicts. Prosecuted for maiestas in 65 and successfully defended by Cicero in a speech known through Asconius' commentary.

people.name: Gaius Manilius
people.summary: Tribune 67/66 who carried the lex Manilia transferring the war against Mithridates and Tigranes to Pompey, supported by Cicero's speech De imperio Cn. Pompei and by Caesar. His bill on freedmen's votes was annulled. Convicted after his tribunate amid riots.

people.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus
people.summary: Consul in 69 who conquered Crete in a brutal three-year war (69-67), clashing with Pompey's legate over the islanders' wish to surrender to Pompey. Kept from his triumph by Pompey's partisans until 62. Grandfather of Caecilia Metella of the famous tomb on the Via Appia.

people.name: Aristobulus II
people.fullName: Aristobulus II, Hasmonean king and high priest

roles.t: King and high priest of Judaea

people.summary: Younger son of Alexander Jannaeus and Salome Alexandra; seized the throne and high priesthood from his brother Hyrcanus in 67. Defied Pompey, was besieged in the Temple in 63, and walked in Pompey's triumph. Escaped twice to raise revolts in Judaea; poisoned by Pompeians in 49 after Caesar freed him.

people.name: Hyrcanus II
people.summary: Elder son of Alexander Jannaeus, high priest under his mother Salome Alexandra (76-67), displaced by his brother in 67 and restored by Pompey in 63 as high priest without the royal title, guided by Antipater. Confirmed as ethnarch by Caesar. Mutilated by Antigonus in 40, he lived in Babylon, returned to Herod's court and was executed by Herod in 30 as a potential rival.

people.name: Antipater the Idumaean
people.summary: Idumaean noble who made himself indispensable to Hyrcanus II and to every Roman commander in the East: Pompey, Scaurus, Gabinius, Caesar. He led 3,000 Jewish troops to relieve Caesar at Alexandria and was rewarded with citizenship and the procuratorship of Judaea. Poisoned at a banquet by a rival, Malichus. Father of Herod.

people.name: Salome Alexandra
people.summary: Widow of Alexander Jannaeus and the only Jewish queen regnant of the Second Temple period (76-67). She reversed her husband's hostility to the Pharisees, gave them control of internal affairs, made her elder son Hyrcanus high priest, and kept peace with Tigranes by diplomacy. Rabbinic memory recalled her reign as a golden age.

people.name: Phraates III
people.summary: Arsacid king of Parthia (c. 70-57) who negotiated with both Lucullus and Pompey, backed his son-in-law Tigranes the Younger against Tigranes II, and was offended when Pompey refused him the title King of Kings. Murdered by his sons Orodes and Mithridates.

people.name: Machares
people.summary: Son of Mithridates VI, made ruler of the Cimmerian Bosporus. He sent Lucullus a golden crown in 70 and made peace with Rome; when his father arrived in 65 he fled to the Tauric Chersonese and killed himself, or was killed.

people.name: Gaius Antonius Hybrida
people.summary: Son of the orator Marcus Antonius and uncle of the triumvir. Expelled from the Senate in 70 for plundering Greece under Sulla, he was nevertheless elected consul with Cicero for 63, after Cicero bought his loyalty with the province of Macedonia. Defeated by the Dardani and Bastarnae, condemned in 59, recalled by Caesar, censor in 42.

people.name: Posidonius
people.summary: Stoic philosopher, polymath and historian from Apamea in Syria who settled at Rhodes, served as its envoy to Rome in 87/86, and taught Cicero; Pompey visited him twice. His History continued Polybius from 146 to the 80s and preserved an ethnography of the Gauls and the Sicilian slave wars that survives through Diodorus, Strabo and Athenaeus. He measured the earth and studied tides at Gades.

people.name: Lucius Licinius Murena
people.summary: Son of the Murena of the Second Mithridatic War, legate of Lucullus in the East, praetor 65, governor of Narbonensis. Elected consul for 62 and prosecuted for bribery by Sulpicius Rufus and Cato; Cicero's Pro Murena won his acquittal.

people.name: Servius Sulpicius Rufus
people.summary: The leading jurist of the late Republic, author of some 180 books, who turned Roman law from practical responses into a systematic science by applying dialectic; his pupils founded the later schools. Consul in 51, he sought compromise in 50-49, accepted Caesar, and governed Achaea. His consolation to Cicero on Tullia's death is famous. Died on an embassy to Antony at Mutina; the Senate voted him a statue on the Rostra.
people.death: died of illness on the embassy to Antony

people.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos
people.summary: Pompey's legate in the East. As tribune in 62 he vetoed Cicero's farewell speech as consul, sought to recall Pompey with his army, was suspended and fled to Pompey. Reconciled with Cicero as consul in 57, when he allowed his recall; governed Nearer Spain.

people.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer
people.summary: Praetor in 63 who blocked Catiline's escape route in Picenum. As consul in 60 he opposed the land bill for Pompey's veterans, though Pompey had divorced his half-sister Mucia, and was imprisoned by the tribune Flavius. Husband of Clodia; his sudden death in 59 was rumoured to be her doing.

people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus
people.summary: Caesar's father-in-law, consul in 58 when he acquiesced in Cicero's exile, then governor of Macedonia (57-55), attacked in Cicero's In Pisonem as a debauched Epicurean. Censor in 50, he tried to mediate in 49 and 44-43 and resisted Antony. Patron of Philodemus and probably owner of the Villa of the Papyri.

people.name: Orgetorix
people.summary: The richest and noblest of the Helvetii, who planned the migration of his people and conspired with Casticus of the Sequani and Dumnorix of the Aedui to seize kingship in their three states. Tried in chains by his people, he came with 10,000 dependants and debtors to overawe the court, then died, Caesar says, probably by suicide.

people.name: Divico
people.summary: Helvetian leader who as a young man led the Tigurini in the defeat of Lucius Cassius at Burdigala in 107 and, aged, headed the Helvetian embassy to Caesar after the battle of the Arar in 58, reminding him of that disaster and declaring that the Helvetii were accustomed to take hostages, not give them.

people.name: Berenice IV
people.summary: Eldest daughter of Ptolemy XII, made queen by the Alexandrians when her father was expelled in 58. She married Archelaus, son of Mithridates' general, who fell fighting Gabinius' army; when Ptolemy XII was restored in 55 he had her executed.

people.name: Marcus Caelius Rufus
people.summary: Brilliant, dissolute protégé of Crassus and Cicero, lover of Clodia, acquitted in 56 with Cicero's Pro Caelio. His letters to Cicero in Cilicia in 51-50 (Ad familiares 8) are the liveliest political reportage from Rome. He joined Caesar in 49, but as praetor in 48 agitated for debt relief and was killed raising revolt near Thurii.
people.death: killed by Caesarian cavalry near Thurii

people.name: Publius Cornelius Lentulus Spinther
people.summary: Consul in 57 who worked for Cicero's recall, then governor of Cilicia hoping to restore Ptolemy XII, a commission blocked by the Sibylline oracle. A friend of Caesar who joined Pompey; pardoned at Corfinium, he fought at Pharsalus and was killed afterward. Nicknamed after an actor he resembled.

people.name: Galba of the Suessiones
people.summary: King of the Suessiones and commander of the Belgic coalition against Caesar in 57, chosen for his justice and wisdom; his predecessor Diviciacus had ruled much of Gaul and Britain. Surrendered his sons as hostages at Noviodunum.

people.name: Clodia Metelli
people.fullName: Clodia, wife of Quintus Metellus Celer
people.summary: Sister of Publius Clodius and wife of Metellus Celer, a wealthy and politically active widow after 59, savaged by Cicero in Pro Caelio as 'the Medea of the Palatine'. Apuleius identifies her with Catullus' Lesbia, and the identification is generally accepted. Still alive in 45, when Cicero considered buying her gardens.

people.name: Quintus Titurius Sabinus
people.summary: Caesar's legate from 58, who defeated the Venelli in 56 by a ruse. In winter 54 he and Cotta commanded a legion and five cohorts at Atuatuca; Sabinus, against Cotta's advice, trusted Ambiorix's offer of safe passage and was killed with nearly all his men.
people.death: killed at a parley with Ambiorix

people.name: Indutiomarus
people.summary: Leader of the anti-Roman faction among the Treveri and rival of his son-in-law Cingetorix. After Atuatuca he incited the Gauls and attacked Labienus' camp, and was killed at a river crossing by Labienus' cavalry, who had orders to hunt him alone.

people.name: Lucterius
people.summary: Cadurcan noble sent by Vercingetorix to raise the Ruteni and threaten the Narbonese province in 52. After Alesia he and the Senonian Drappes held Uxellodunum; Lucterius was later handed over to Caesar by the Arvernian Epasnactus.

people.name: Litaviccus
people.summary: Young Aeduan noble who in 52 led the Aeduan contingent marching to Caesar into revolt with a false story of Caesar's massacre of Aeduan leaders, then fled to Vercingetorix at Gergovia. His agitation brought the Aedui into the general revolt.

people.name: Drappes
people.summary: Senonian adventurer who with Lucterius led the remnant of the western rebels into Uxellodunum in 51. Captured during the siege, he starved himself to death.

people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus (consul 51)
people.summary: Consul in 51 and leader of the hardline attempts to recall Caesar from Gaul; flogged a magistrate of Novum Comum to deny Caesar's grants of citizenship. After Pharsalus he lived in exile at Mytilene; pardoned by Caesar in 46 at the Senate's request, prompting Cicero's Pro Marcello, he was murdered at Piraeus on his way home by a friend.
people.death: murdered at Piraeus by his companion Magius Cilo

people.name: Pothinus
people.summary: Eunuch regent of the young Ptolemy XIII who drove out Cleopatra and, with Achillas and the rhetor Theodotus, decided on the murder of Pompey. Caesar had him executed when he was found plotting during the Alexandrian War.

people.name: Achillas
people.summary: Commander of Ptolemy XIII's army who personally carried out the murder of Pompey at Pelusium with the Roman officers Septimius and Salvius, then besieged Caesar in Alexandria with 20,000 men, many of them Gabinius' former Roman soldiers. Murdered by Arsinoe IV's eunuch Ganymedes.
people.death: killed by Ganymedes on Arsinoe's orders

people.name: Publius Cornelius Dolabella (consul 44)
people.summary: Patrician rake who married Cicero's daughter Tullia in 50 (divorced 46), joined Caesar, lost a fleet in Illyricum in 49, and as tribune in 47 agitated for debt cancellation. Caesar named him suffect consul for 44 over Antony's objections; after the Ides he courted the Liberators, then seized Syria, murdering Trebonius on the way. Besieged by Cassius at Laodicea, he had a soldier kill him.

people.name: Publius Sittius
people.summary: Campanian financier, suspected of involvement with Catiline, who fled his debts in 64 to Mauretania and became a mercenary captain there. In 46 he and Bocchus II attacked Juba's kingdom, took Cirta and destroyed Metellus Scipio's fleet. Caesar gave him and his men the territory of Cirta; he was murdered by a Numidian noble in 44.
people.death: assassinated by Arabio, son of Masinissa II

people.name: Marcus Petreius
people.summary: A professional soldier of thirty years' service who commanded the army that destroyed Catiline at Pistoria in 62 when the consul Antonius pleaded gout. Pompey's legate in Spain with Afranius in 49, he fought on in Africa and killed himself with Juba after Thapsus.

people.name: Mithridates of Pergamon
people.summary: Son of a Galatian tetrarch's daughter, claimed as a natural son of Mithridates VI. He raised the relief army that saved Caesar in Alexandria in 47, storming Pelusium, and was rewarded with the Bosporan kingdom and part of Galatia, but was killed trying to take the Bosporus from Asander.

people.name: Ptolemy XIV
people.summary: Younger brother of Cleopatra, made co-ruler and nominal husband by Caesar in 47 after Ptolemy XIII drowned. He accompanied Cleopatra to Rome and died in summer 44, probably poisoned on her orders to clear the way for Caesarion.

people.name: Tullia
people.summary: Cicero's beloved daughter, married to Gaius Calpurnius Piso Frugi, Furius Crassipes and Publius Dolabella. She died at Tusculum in February 45, a month after giving birth to Dolabella's son. Cicero's grief led him to plan a shrine (fanum) to her and to write a Consolatio, and drove his philosophical writing.

people.name: Titus Pomponius Atticus
people.fullName: Titus Pomponius Atticus (Quintus Caecilius Pomponianus Atticus)
people.summary: Equestrian banker, publisher and antiquarian, Cicero's closest friend and the recipient of 16 books of his letters. Living in Athens from 85 to 65 (hence his cognomen), he refused all office and stayed on good terms with every faction from Sulla to Antony and Octavian; his daughter married Agrippa. He starved himself to death when terminally ill.
people.detail: Atticus is the great example of a Roman who prospered by staying out of politics: he lent money to Marius' son and to Brutus, protected Fulvia when Antony was outlawed, and was spared in the proscriptions because of it. His Liber Annalis, a chronological table of Roman history, was used by Cicero and Nepos. His slaves copied and distributed Cicero's works. Nepos' Life of him is an admiring portrait by a friend.

people.name: Aulus Hirtius
people.summary: Caesar's officer and literary aide, who wrote the eighth book of the Gallic War to bridge Caesar's commentaries and probably edited the Alexandrian War. Praetor 46, he struck Caesar's great gold issue. As consul in 43 he fell in the victory outside Mutina; he and his colleague Pansa were given a public funeral.
people.death: killed storming Antony's camp at Mutina

people.name: Gaius Vibius Pansa Caetronianus
people.summary: Son of a proscribed Marian, a loyal Caesarian, governor of Bithynia and Cisalpine Gaul, and consul with Hirtius in 43. Wounded at Forum Gallorum leading recruits against Antony, he died at Bononia days later; rumour accused Octavian of having his wounds poisoned.
people.death: died of wounds after Forum Gallorum

people.name: Lucius Munatius Plancus
people.summary: Caesar's legate in Gaul and the civil war, governor of Gallia Comata in 44-43, founder of Lugdunum and Raurica, who wavered elegantly before joining Antony in 43. Consul 42, he followed Antony to the East, then defected to Octavian in 32 and revealed Antony's will. In 27 he proposed the name Augustus; censor in 22. His tomb survives at Gaeta.
people.detail: Velleius calls him a 'morbid traitor'. He was said to have performed in Alexandria as the sea god Glaucus, painted blue and naked, crawling on his knees at a banquet of Antony and Cleopatra. Yet he was among the most successful survivors of the age, rebuilt the Temple of Saturn, and Horace addressed an ode to him.

people.name: Gaius Asinius Pollio
people.summary: Marrucinian new man, Caesar's officer at the Rubicon and Pharsalus, governor of Further Spain in 44-43, who joined Antony and as consul in 40 helped negotiate the Treaty of Brundisium. After triumphing over the Parthini he withdrew from politics, founded Rome's first public library, introduced public readings (recitationes), and wrote a history of the civil wars from 60 used by Appian and Plutarch. Patron of Virgil.
people.detail: Pollio cultivated independence: he refused to join Octavian at Actium, saying he would be the prize of the victor, and as a critic he called Caesar's commentaries careless and Livy's style provincial ('Patavinitas'). Horace's Ode 2.1 warns him that writing the history of the civil wars was walking on fire hidden under ash.

people.name: Quintus Salvidienus Rufus
people.summary: Of humble origins, a companion of the young Octavian at Apollonia, his first general against Sextus Pompey and at Perusia, governor of Gaul with eleven legions and consul designate for 39. Denounced by Antony at Brundisium for proposing to defect, he was condemned by the Senate and killed himself or was executed.
people.death: condemned as a public enemy; suicide or execution

people.name: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus (consul 32)
people.summary: Son of Caesar's enemy Lucius Domitius, captured at Corfinium and pardoned. Condemned under the lex Pedia though probably not a conspirator, he commanded the Liberators' fleet, destroyed the triumviral convoy on the day of Philippi, then made peace with Antony. Consul in 32, he fled to Antony, opposed Cleopatra's presence, and deserted to Octavian just before Actium, dying soon after. Great-grandfather of Nero.
people.death: died of illness shortly after deserting to Octavian

people.name: Gaius Sosius
people.summary: Antony's governor of Syria who with Herod took Jerusalem in 37 and triumphed in 34. As consul in 32 he denounced Octavian in the Senate and fled to Antony; commanded the left wing of Antony's fleet at Actium. Pardoned by Octavian at Arruntius' request, he rebuilt the Temple of Apollo Medicus (Apollo Sosianus), whose restored columns stand near the Theatre of Marcellus.

people.name: Gaius Trebonius
people.summary: Tribune of 55 whose lex Trebonia gave Pompey and Crassus their five-year commands, then Caesar's legate in Gaul who commanded the siege of Massilia. Suffect consul 45, he joined the conspiracy and detained Antony outside the Senate on the Ides. Murdered by Dolabella at Smyrna as proconsul of Asia, the first of the assassins to die.

people.name: Antigonus II Mattathias

roles.t: King and high priest of Judaea

people.summary: Son of Aristobulus II, twice a fugitive from Roman custody, who with Parthian backing took Jerusalem in 40 and reigned as king and high priest, mutilating his uncle Hyrcanus. Besieged by Herod and Sosius in 37, he surrendered and was beheaded by Antony at Antioch, the last Hasmonean ruler.
people.death: beheaded at Antioch on Antony's orders

people.name: Arsinoe IV
people.summary: Younger sister of Cleopatra who escaped Caesar's palace during the Alexandrian War, was proclaimed queen by the Alexandrian army, and had Achillas killed. Captured, she walked in Caesar's triumph of 46, where her dignity moved the crowd, and was allowed into sanctuary at Ephesus until Antony had her killed in 41.
people.death: killed at Ephesus on Antony's orders

people.name: Gaius Licinius Macer Calvus
people.summary: Son of the tribune-historian Licinius Macer, a tiny man and fierce Atticist orator who prosecuted Vatinius, and a neoteric poet, Catullus' closest friend, author of an epyllion Io and an elegy for his wife Quintilia. Only fragments survive.

people.name: Gaius Helvius Cinna
people.summary: Neoteric poet from Brixia or nearby, friend of Catullus, whose learned epyllion Zmyrna took nine years to write. As tribune in 44 he was mistaken for the anti-Caesarian praetor Lucius Cinna and lynched by the crowd at Caesar's funeral.
people.death: lynched by mistake at Caesar's funeral

people.name: Cornelius Nepos
people.summary: Biographer from Cisalpine Gaul, friend of Atticus and Cicero and dedicatee of Catullus' book. His Chronica summarised world history in three books; his De viris illustribus, partly extant, is the oldest surviving Latin biography. He refused a political career.

people.name: Diodorus Siculus
people.summary: Sicilian Greek who spent thirty years on a forty-book universal history, the Bibliotheca, ending with Caesar's Gallic War; he visited Egypt in the 180th Olympiad (60-56) and lived in Rome. A compiler rather than a critic, he is precious for preserving lost sources: Hecataeus of Abdera, Agatharchides, Timaeus, Posidonius.

people.name: Philodemus of Gadara
people.summary: Epicurean philosopher and epigrammatist from Gadara in the Decapolis, pupil of Zeno of Sidon, who lived in Italy under the patronage of Piso Caesoninus and taught Virgil, Varius and others in the circle at Naples and Herculaneum. Many of his treatises survive charred among the papyri of the Villa of the Papyri; some thirty of his erotic epigrams are in the Greek Anthology.

people.name: Servilia
people.summary: Half-sister of Cato the Younger, mother of Marcus Brutus by her first husband and of three daughters by Decimus Silanus, consul 62. Caesar's most famous mistress, to whom he gave a pearl worth six million sesterces. After the Ides she chaired a family council at Antium in June 44 that discussed the Liberators' future, with Cicero present.

people.name: Terentia
people.summary: Cicero's wealthy and forceful wife, half-sister of a Vestal, who managed his property during his exile and, Plutarch says, urged him to act against the Catilinarians and to testify against Clodius. They divorced in 47/46 amid quarrels over money; she reputedly lived to 103.

people.name: Marcus Tullius Tiro
people.summary: Cicero's slave, freed in 53, his secretary and literary executor, who edited and published Cicero's letters and speeches, collected his jokes, wrote his biography, and developed or perfected the Latin shorthand system ('Tironian notes') used into the Middle Ages.

people.name: Atia
people.summary: Daughter of Julia, Caesar's sister, and Marcus Atius Balbus; mother of Octavia and of Octavian by Gaius Octavius, and later wife of Lucius Marcius Philippus. Tacitus praises her strict upbringing of her son; she urged caution when he accepted Caesar's inheritance. Died during his first consulship.

people.name: Scribonia
people.summary: Sister of Lucius Scribonius Libo, Sextus Pompey's father-in-law; married Octavian in 40 to win Sextus' goodwill, bore Julia, and was divorced on the day of Julia's birth in 39 so that Octavian could marry Livia. She later chose to accompany Julia into exile on Pandateria.

people.name: Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus
people.summary: Patrician who fought for the Liberators at Philippi, then joined Antony and finally Octavian, commanding at Naulochus and Actium. Consul in 31, he triumphed over Aquitania in 27, was briefly first prefect of the city (26), and proposed the title Pater Patriae (2 BC). Orator, patron of Tibullus and Ovid.

people.name: Publius Canidius Crassus
people.summary: Antony's general who conquered the Iberians and Albanians of the Caucasus in 36 and commanded his land army at Actium. He advised Antony to send Cleopatra home and fight on land, and after the naval defeat abandoned the army, which surrendered. Executed by Octavian after Alexandria.

people.name: Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta
people.summary: Caesar's legate who shared command at Atuatuca with Sabinus in winter 54 and argued against leaving camp on Ambiorix's word. When the column was ambushed he fought on, wounded in the face by a sling bullet, and died with most of his men.
people.death: killed in the ambush at Atuatuca

people.name: Catuvolcus
people.summary: Elderly co-king of the Eburones with Ambiorix, who joined the attack on Sabinus and Cotta in 54. When Caesar ravaged his country in 53 he cursed Ambiorix and poisoned himself with yew.

people.name: Vercassivellaunus
people.summary: Cousin of Vercingetorix and one of the four commanders of the Gallic relief army at Alesia. He led 60,000 picked men in the decisive attack on the weak point of Caesar's northern lines on Mont Réa and was captured when the attack failed.

people.name: Boduognatus
people.summary: Commander of the Nervii who led the surprise attack on Caesar's army at the Sabis in 57, which nearly destroyed it; Caesar says that the Nervii were all but annihilated in the battle.

people.name: Antiochus XIII Asiaticus
people.summary: Son of Antiochus X and Cleopatra Selene, who lobbied the Senate in Rome in the 70s for recognition of his claim to Egypt; Verres robbed him in Sicily on his way home. Installed in Antioch by Lucullus after 69, he was deposed by Pompey in 64, ending Seleucid rule, and murdered by the Emesene dynast Sampsiceramus.

people.name: Taxiles
people.summary: Mithridates' general who brought an army of some 100,000 to join Archelaus in Greece in 86 and shared the command at Chaeronea, and later led the cavalry against Lucullus at Cabira and fought at Tigranocerta.

people.name: Publius Nigidius Figulus
people.summary: Praetor in 58, a Pompeian, and, after Varro, the most learned Roman of his age: a Neo-Pythagorean scholar of grammar, astrology, natural science and divination, consulted by Cicero in 63. Legend said he cast Octavian's horoscope on the day of his birth and announced a ruler of the world. Died in exile.
people.death: died in exile, unpardoned by Caesar

people.name: Sosigenes of Alexandria
people.summary: Peripatetic astronomer whom Pliny names as Caesar's adviser for the calendar reform of 46, which adopted a solar year of 365 days with a leap day every fourth year, based on Egyptian practice. He also wrote on the planets.

people.name: Lucius Hirtuleius
people.summary: Sertorius' quaestor and best lieutenant, who defeated the governor of Narbonensis, Manlius, at Ilerda in 78 and held Metellus Pius in check, but was destroyed by Metellus at Italica in 76 and killed near Segovia in 75.
people.death: killed in battle against Metellus Pius

people.name: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus Crus
people.summary: Consul in 49, heavily in debt, who refused to read Caesar's last proposals to the Senate, carried the senatus consultum ultimum of 7 January and fled Rome leaving the treasury unopened. After Pharsalus he followed Pompey to Egypt and was killed in prison there.
people.death: put to death in Egypt after Pompey's murder

people.name: Gaius Scribonius Curio (consul 76)
people.summary: Sulla's legate in Greece, consul 76 and the first Roman general to reach the Danube, campaigning against the Dardani in 75-73. An orator of Cicero's acquaintance and enemy of Caesar, he wrote a dialogue attacking Caesar's consulship and called him 'every woman's husband and every man's wife'. Father of the tribune of 50.

people.name: Gaius Memmius (praetor 58)
people.summary: Praetor in 58 who attacked Caesar's consular acts, governor of Bithynia in 57 with Catullus and Helvius Cinna on his staff, and dedicatee of Lucretius' De rerum natura. As consular candidate in 54 he exposed in the Senate the corrupt pact he had made with the consuls, ending his career; convicted of ambitus, he retired to Athens, where he planned to demolish Epicurus' house, to Cicero's dismay.
